summary.text: At \(n=9\), direct evaluation gives \(a(9)=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901=29^2\cdot 59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\), so this term is not squarefree; that single counterexample falsifies the conjunction regardless of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let the primes be indexed starting at zero:
\[
p_0=2,\quad p_1=3,\quad p_2=5,\quad\ldots,
\]
and define the corresponding primorial and sequence term by
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\qquad
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
Thus \(P_n\) is the product of the first \(n\) primes; in particular, the empty product gives \(P_0=1\) and \(a(0)=2\).

We disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by considering \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Indeed, these numbers are prime, and all intervening integers from \(2\) through \(23\) are composite: the omitted integers greater than one are
\[
4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15,16,18,20,21,22,
\]
with their compositeness immediate from divisibility by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\), or \(7\). Consequently,
\[
P_9=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23.
\]
Multiplying successively gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot3&=6,\\
6\cdot5&=30,\\
30\cdot7&=210,\\
210\cdot11&=2310,\\
2310\cdot13&=30030,\\
30030\cdot17&=510510,\\
510510\cdot19&=9699690,\\
9699690\cdot23&=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
P_9=223092870
\]
and therefore
\[
a(9)=223092870^2+1=49770428644836901.
\]

Now consider the square \(29^2=841\). There is a particularly short modular check that this square divides \(a(9)\). We have the exact division
\[
223092870=841\cdot265270+800.
\]
Since \(800\equiv-41\pmod{841}\), it follows that
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1681+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Thus
\[
29^2=841\mid a(9).
\]
For completeness, the corresponding exact factorization is
\[
49770428644836901
 =841\cdot59180057841661.
\]
The multiplication on the right can also be checked directly by writing \(841=800+40+1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
59180057841661\cdot800&=47344046273328800,\\
59180057841661\cdot40&=2367202313666440,\\
59180057841661\cdot1&=59180057841661,
\end{aligned}
\]
and the sum of these three numbers is \(49770428644836901\).

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when no square \(d^2\) with \(d>1\) divides it (equivalently, when no prime square divides it). Here \(29>1\), yet \(29^2\mid a(9)\), so \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. If one uses the equivalent formulation in terms of prime squares, note that \(29\) is prime: a composite divisor test only needs the primes at most \(\sqrt{29}<6\), and \(29\) is divisible by none of \(2,3,5\).

Therefore the universal claim
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false, with the explicit counterexample \(n=9\).

The stated conjecture is the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness assertion and the assertion that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction cannot hold when one of its conjuncts is false. Hence
\[
\neg\left(\bigl(\forall n,\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree}\bigr)
\ \wedge\
\bigl(\{n:a(n)\text{ is prime}\}\text{ is infinite}\bigr)\right).
\]
This disproves the combined conjecture. The counterexample settles the squarefreeness part negatively; no conclusion about the separate infinitude-of-primes assertion is needed.
